Chapter 4: Faith in Action—Peacemaking and Nonviolence
You know, in a world that’s so often marked by conflict and division, the idea of being a peacemaker can honestly sound a little naive—or maybe even impossible. Most of us grow up hearing that violence is just part of life, that sometimes, it’s necessary.
But if you really pay attention to the teachings of Jesus, there’s this powerful call to love our enemies and seek out reconciliation. That’s not just about changing how we feel on the inside. It invites us to rethink the very systems and habits that shape our whole society.
The friends who lived in community learned this firsthand—and, honestly, in some pretty unexpected ways. Their neighborhood wasn’t exactly peaceful: arguments, fights, and the constant threat of harm showed up almost every day. At first, it was tempting to just keep their distance, not get involved.
But as they started building real relationships with their neighbors, they realized peacemaking wasn’t just some lofty idea. It was something you had to practice, day in and day out—as much a part of daily life as sharing a meal or saying hello.
One afternoon, a fight broke out right there on the street. Now, instead of turning away, one of the friends decided to step in—not with shouting, not with threats, but with calm words and a willingness to listen. And you know what? The tension eased, and that conflict just melted away.
It was such a clear reminder: sometimes, just showing up and refusing to add fuel to the fire can really change everything.
That experience got the friends thinking even more deeply about the bigger picture—the way our culture often normalizes violence, whether it’s war, injustice, or just the hurtful things people say and do to each other. It’s so easy to believe, “Well, that’s just the way things are.” But the teachings of Jesus? They point to something completely different—a path of forgiveness, of reconciliation, of creative resistance.
Inspired by stories of nonviolent movements all over the world, the friends started looking for ways to live this out. They joined protests against war, stood by those struggling with injustice, and tried to build bridges between groups that didn’t trust each other. It wasn’t always simple. In fact, they faced a lot of criticism—some folks even thought their actions were foolish or unpatriotic.
But the more they leaned into peacemaking, the more they saw its quiet power. Small acts of courage—like refusing to hit back, offering a kind word, or standing with someone who’s vulnerable—those moments started to ripple out. The neighborhood slowly became a little safer, maybe even a little more hopeful. People who’d once been enemies began to find common ground. Old wounds started to heal.
Most people underestimate what nonviolence can actually do. The friends discovered that peacemaking doesn’t mean being passive or just avoiding tough situations. It’s about actively seeking the good of others, even when it costs you something. It means standing up to injustice, but doing it with love instead of hate.
And let’s be honest—the journey toward nonviolence isn’t easy. There were moments when the friends felt afraid, angry, or full of doubt. But every time they chose peace over violence, they caught a glimpse of a different kind of world—a world where love really is stronger than fear, and where ordinary people—people just like you and me—can make a real difference.
